Nauseous relates to nausea — that deeply uncomfortable, queasy feeling in your stomach that makes you feel like you might vomit. The adjective "nauseous" describes something that is connected to that feeling, either by causing it or by experiencing it.

Here is where it gets interesting, and where even educated native speakers get confused. The word "nauseous" has two valid meanings, and understanding both will make you sharper than most people.

Meaning 1 — Causing nausea (the traditional meaning)

In its original, classical sense, nauseous describes something outside of you — a thing, a smell, a sight, a situation — that produces the feeling of nausea in whoever encounters it. The nauseous thing is the source of the sickness, not the victim of it.

"The nauseous stench from the garbage bin drove everyone away."
(The stench is so disgusting it makes people feel sick.)

"There was a nauseous smell of chemicals in the laboratory."
(The smell causes nausea.)

"The graphic video was nauseous — most viewers had to look away."
(It produced a feeling of disgust and sickness.)

Think of it this way: if something is nauseous, it has the power to make you feel sick.

Meaning 2 — Feeling nausea (the modern, widely accepted meaning)

In everyday modern usage — and now fully accepted by most major dictionaries — nauseous also describes a person (or animal) who feels sick to their stomach. Here, the nauseous one is the victim of the feeling, not the cause.

"She felt nauseous after riding the roller coaster."
(Her stomach felt awful; she felt like she might vomit.)

"I'm nauseous — I think I ate something bad."
(I am experiencing that sick, queasy feeling.)

"The patient became nauseous following the chemotherapy."
(He started feeling sick to his stomach.)
Why Two Meanings? And Which One Should You Use?

Language evolves. So many people used "nauseous" to mean "feeling sick" over so many decades that dictionaries eventually accepted this usage as correct. Today, both meanings are standard English. You will not be wrong in formal or informal settings using either one, as long as the context makes your meaning clear.

That said, careful writers and editors — particularly in formal, academic, or professional writing — still prefer to make a distinction:

  • Use nauseous for the cause → "The fumes were nauseous."
  • Use nauseated for the person feeling sick → "I felt nauseated by the fumes."

This keeps the two ideas cleanly separated and avoids any ambiguity.
The Closely Related Words You Must Know

To fully understand "nauseous," you need to know its family members:

1. Nauseated (adjective/past participle)
This describes a person who feels nausea. It is the precise, unambiguous word for the experiencer of nausea.

"She was nauseated by the smell." → She felt sick.

2. Nauseating (adjective)
This describes something that causes nausea. It is the precise, unambiguous word for the source of nausea.

"The smell was nauseating." → The smell caused sickness.

3. Nausea (noun)
The actual feeling — that awful, queasy sensation in the stomach.

"She was overcome with nausea."

Quick summary of the family:

  • The smell is nauseating (it causes sickness) → it is nauseous (same idea)
  • You feel nauseated (you experience sickness) → you feel nauseous (same idea, widely accepted)

"Nauseous" is a gradable adjective, meaning you can express different degrees of the feeling or quality:

"slightly nauseous" — a mild, passing queasiness
"quite nauseous" — noticeably unwell
"extremely nauseous" — severely sick, on the verge of vomiting

Here are the most natural ways "nauseous" appears in real English:

  • "feel nauseous" → "I started to feel nauseous on the boat."
  • "become nauseous" → "She became nauseous during the surgery."
  • "make someone nauseous" → "The smell makes me nauseous."
  • "a nauseous smell/feeling/sensation" → "There was a nauseous odor in the room."
  • "look nauseous" → "You look nauseous — are you okay?"
One Sentence to Remember It All
Nauseous means either causing that horrible sick-to-your-stomach feeling, or having that horrible sick-to-your-stomach feeling — and in modern English, both uses are correct.

Read these two sentences. Both are correct, and now you know exactly why:

  1. "The rollercoaster was so nauseous that three people vomited."

(The rollercoaster caused nausea — traditional meaning.)

  1. "I felt nauseous after riding the rollercoaster."

(I experienced nausea — modern accepted meaning.)

If you can read those two sentences and understand the slight difference in perspective each one carries, you have fully mastered the word nauseous.
